title: On one foot (Shabbat 31a)
hook: a man asks Hillel for the whole Torah on one foot: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; go and learn

segments.voice: Yesterday the Talmud's very first question was about the evening Shema. Your line was when does evening start. Did you catch the moment your evening began? Day two hundred seventy-two.

You've heard someone say it. Give me the short version. Explain your job in one sentence. Sum up the whole book in a tweet. It's usually a little impatient, and a little unfair. Long ago, a man who wasn't Jewish walked up to Hillel, one of the great sages of his day, and made an impatient request. Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Everything. Before I lose my balance. Today we hear what Hillel said, and the line after it that often gets dropped.
screen: `GIVE ME THE SHORT VERSION.` → `THE WHOLE TORAH?` → `WHILE I STAND ON ONE FOOT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page 31a. The man says he'll convert if Hillel can teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel doesn't laugh and doesn't send him away. He accepts him, and says, in Aramaic: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is its commentary. Go and learn it. Three moves. First, the rule itself. It echoes the Torah's own words, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," from Leviticus. But Hillel turns it around into something anyone can check. You may not always know what love asks of you. You almost always know what hurts. Start there. Second: the rest is commentary. Hillel doesn't say the rest doesn't matter. The Sabbath, the festivals, the food laws, the prayers: he calls all of it the explanation, the working-out of that one rule in real life. Third, and this is the part people drop: go and learn. The summary fits on one foot. Living it takes both feet and the rest of your life. Hillel gives the man a door, not a shortcut. And notice who he says it to: an outsider, impatient, maybe a little rude. The whole Torah on one foot is also a lesson in how to answer a question like that.
screen: `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU…` · `DON'T DO IT TO YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` · `GO AND LEARN.` · then, large: `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's hateful thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that really stings when someone does it to you. Being interrupted. Being talked about. Being left on read. Being corrected in front of people. Pick one. Now picture where in your day you might be tempted to do that same thing to someone else. See the moment clearly. Then picture yourself not doing it. That's Hillel's rule, lived for one day. The bell holds the time.
Hillel, who agreed to teach the whole Torah while a man stood on one foot: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. The rest is commentary. Go and learn.
Your line: the rest is commentary. Today, live by one rule: don't do to anyone the thing that stings you. Day two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Hillel's answer is often taught to children, quoted in sermons, and paired with the Torah's command to love your neighbor as yourself.

fork.setup: you're a teacher. a stranger says: teach me your whole tradition while I stand on one foot. what do you do?
options: send him away. it's a rude question.
give him one sentence, then: go and learn.
tell him it can't be summed up.
fork.reveal: Hillel gave him one sentence, what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, and then sent him to learn the rest.

original.note: Aramaic: go and learn. the last words of Hillel's answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the golden rule in a nutshell.
what it means: one rule, and everything else is how you live it. then: go and learn.
what a scholar hears: Hillel says it in Aramaic and in the negative, and his word for neighbor, chavrach, means your fellow, your friend.

sources.quoted: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the date 'two thousand years ago' and the superlative 'the most impatient request of all'; 'three words' count dropped (Hillel's Aramaic zil gemor is two words), here and in the match pair; howItsDone superlative removed.
Shabbat 31a paraphrased. The Aramaic is often rendered: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow (chavrach).
Trapdoor floor 3: confirm chavrach (your fellow) in the Aramaic of Shabbat 31a.
Some readers see Hillel's 'the whole Torah' as a teaching tool, not a claim that ritual law is secondary; the script says so.
